turns.name: W2-dyn
turns.question: You said the app saves the intent with a client transfer ID before sending — what exactly gets written to local storage at that moment, and how does the app use that ID when the response comes back?

card.problem: Design a mobile wallet: core mobile experience, the system behind it, and how it handles failures
card.adopted: Server ledger is the single source of truth; the phone keeps a local copy for cached reads
card.constraints: ["Start by clarifying the requirements and define the MVP user path", "Signed-in users, centralized balance accounts, single currency USD, internal peer-to-peer transfers, zero fees", "Balance, transfer, history and details in scope; cached reads work", "Offline submitting money needs the network; the server owns the authoritative ledger", "Ledger limits, top up, withdrawal and multi-currency are out of scope; A has 100 dollars and B has 0"]
card.heard: what gets written locally, at that moment, and how the ID is used on response
card.say: I write one row in the local database: the client transfer ID, the recipient, the amount as 8000 cents, and the status "pending". I write it before the request goes out, so the intent survives a crash or process death. When the response comes back, I look up that row by the same ID and update its status to success or failure. The result screen reads only from that row, so a late or duplicate response just updates the same record.
card.then: Next, the lost-response case: timeout, app restart, and the lookup by client transfer ID.

more: When the response comes back, I match it to that row by the client transfer ID. Then I update the status to success or clear failure, and the result screen reads only from that row. If the response never comes, the row stays pending, so it's an unknown outcome, not a failure. After a restart I ask the server for that same ID, and I resend only that ID, only if the server's contract allows it.

card.say: For the first version, I'd ship balance, internal transfer, history and details. I'd also include the native confirmation step and the pending and unknown states. Before release, I'd test the cases we discussed: a lost response with a process kill, a replay of the same client ID, two transfers at once, and an account switch mid-flight. I'd look at the error rate and the server's response times for the transfer and lookup calls. If the server is slow or failing, I'd pause new submissions and keep the lookup running, so pending rows can still resolve. Then I'd tell the product owner and the tech lead what I saw and what I paused.

transcript: Interviewer: Hi, I'm the founder of ActAI. We're building an agent-first mobile communication app, focused on how people talk, coordinate and work together every day. Today we'll start with a project you really owned, then design a fictional mobile wallet together. I'll add a few new conditions along the way, and leave time for your questions at the end.
Interviewer: Pick the one project that best shows your mobile skills. Who used it, what problem did it solve, and where did your responsibility start and end?
Candidate: The users were travelers on the KKday app, mostly in Asia.
Candidate: They wanted to book tours and activities at their destination.
Candidate: Planning by hand took a lot of time.
Candidate: They had to work out the budget, search products one by one, and put the plan together.
Candidate: So the AI did that for them.
Candidate: I designed the agent and the backend, agreed the response format with the app team, and wrote the Android code that reads the streamed plan.
Candidate: The product team owned the final user experience, and I made their decisions work.

Interviewer: On the KKday AI planning project, you said you designed the agent and backend and wrote the Android code that reads the streamed plan — which exact pieces did you build yourself, and which parts did the app team or product team own?
Candidate: I built the agent design, the core backend, and the Android code that reads the streamed plan.
Candidate: The app team built the screens and the day cards.
Candidate: The product team owned the final user experience, and I made their decisions work.
Interviewer: Pick a change you personally made. Walk me from one user action through the UI, data or network path. Which logic did you actually change?
Candidate: The change I made was on the Android side, in how the app reads the streamed plan.
Candidate: Before, the app waited for the whole plan, then showed it.
Candidate: I changed it to read the SSE stream and show each day card as it arrives.
Candidate: So the user sees Day 1 first, while the rest is still being made.
Candidate: The user types "Tokyo, 5,000 yuan, three days" and taps send.
Candidate: The app opens an SSE connection to our backend.
Candidate: The backend runs the agent, and each finished day comes back as one event.
Candidate: The list is backed by StateFlow, so Compose redraws as each day arrives.
Candidate: Parsing and JSON work run on Dispatchers.Default, not the main thread.
Interviewer: What was the hardest bug to reproduce there? What did you suspect first, and which log, experiment or repro proved you wrong?
Candidate: The hardest bug was a day card that sometimes showed the wrong price.
Candidate: It only happened when two events arrived close together.
Candidate: I first suspected the backend sent bad data.
Candidate: Then I logged the raw events and saw the order was fine.
Candidate: The real cause was on my side: two updates raced, and the older one overwrote the newer one.
Candidate: I added a regression test that replays the two events in the failing order, and I capped the pending-event buffer so a stalled stream can't grow it without bound.

Interviewer: You said the older update overwrote the newer one — how did you actually confirm that was the root cause rather than just a plausible theory, and how did you verify the fix held up after release?
Candidate: I confirmed it with a log of the raw events and their timestamps.
Candidate: The order was fine, but the two updates reached the list out of order.
Candidate: So the theory was wrong, and the race was real.
Candidate: I also replayed the two events in the failing order on my machine.
Candidate: It failed every time, and it passed after the fix.
Candidate: The replay test only covers the two-event order we saw, so a three-way interleaving with a third update could still slip through.
Interviewer: What other options did you have, why didn't you pick them, and after release how did you know the change worked?
Candidate: I had two other options.
Candidate: First, I could drop any event older than the last one I showed, using a sequence number.
Candidate: Second, I could keep a small buffer and apply events in order.
Candidate: I didn't pick the buffer alone, because a stalled stream could still grow it.
Candidate: So I used the sequence number as the main fix, and capped the buffer as a safety net.
Candidate: After release, I watched the crash-free rate and the error logs for that screen.
Candidate: I also checked that no day card showed a price that didn't match the product data.
Candidate: The replay test stayed in the build, so the same order can't come back quietly.
Candidate: I also checked how often a day card showed a price that didn't match the final plan.
Candidate: If that number went up, I'd pause the rollout and go back to the old behaviour while we looked into it.

Interviewer: Tell me about a time you saw a delivery risk or a likely delay and the team disagreed. When did you tell whom, how many options did you give, who decided, and what did you finish yourself?
Candidate: At Debon Securities, I was moving part of our trading app to the new navigation.
Candidate: It was planned for that week's release.
Candidate: During testing I found some old pages had a broken back button.
Candidate: I told the project manager the same day, before I had checked every page.
Candidate: I gave two options: keep the old pages and move my change to the next release, or ship it and accept the risk.
Candidate: He decided to keep the old pages.
Candidate: Everything else shipped on time.
Candidate: I finished the fix and the testing myself, and my change went out in the next release.

Interviewer: You said the PM chose to keep the old pages and ship everything else on time — what risk were you personally willing to accept there, and who was watching the data after that release? What signal would have made you pause or roll back?
Candidate: I was willing to take the risk of my own change slipping, not the risk of a broken back button reaching users.
Candidate: So I said clearly that I'd rather ship it late than ship it broken.
Candidate: For that release, the project manager and I watched the crash reports in Bugly and the error logs for the pages I'd touched.
Candidate: I checked them every day for the first week.
Candidate: The signal that would have made me pause was a rise in crashes or back-button errors on those pages.
Candidate: If that happened, I'd ask to turn the change off and go back to the old pages while we fixed it.

Interviewer: Let's switch to the design exercise. Design a mobile wallet from scratch: the core mobile experience, the system behind it, and how it handles failures. Start by clarifying the requirements. Which user path would you define as the MVP?
Candidate: Before I design, a few questions.
Candidate: Is the balance held by us, or does money move on a bank or card rail?
Candidate: Which currencies do we support?
Candidate: What should work offline?
Candidate: And is the server ledger the single source of truth?
Candidate: Does that match what you want first?
Candidate: I'd start with one path: send money to a contact, and see the balance update.
Candidate: That's the MVP.
Candidate: For the rest, I'd assume the server ledger holds the truth, and the phone keeps a local copy for offline viewing.
Candidate: I'd confirm that with you.

Interviewer: Here are the rules: signed-in users, centralized balance accounts, single currency USD, internal peer-to-peer transfers, zero fees. Balance, transfer, history and details are in scope. Cached reads work offline; submitting money needs the network. The server owns the authoritative ledger and limits. Top-up, withdrawal and multi-currency are out of scope. A has 100 dollars and B has zero. Draw the client, the server and local storage as a flowchart, and tell me what each part owns.
Candidate: Okay, the rules are clear.
Candidate: The server ledger is the single source of truth.
Candidate: The phone keeps a local copy for cached reads.
Candidate: The client never decides a balance on its own.
Candidate: Here's the flow.

[board] flowchart TD |   A[Screen: balance and transfer form] --> B[ViewModel: state and send] |   B --> C[Repository] |   C --> D[Local database: cached copy] |   C --> E[Server: ledger, source of truth] |   E --> C |   C --> D
Candidate: The screen only shows state and sends the user's action.
Candidate: The ViewModel holds the UI state and calls the repository.
Candidate: The repository is the only door to data.
Candidate: It reads the cached copy for display and sends transfers to the server.
Candidate: The local database is just a cached copy for offline reads.
Interviewer: Now draw a sequence diagram of A sending B 80 dollars: confirmation, request, ledger and the result screen.
Candidate: Here's the sequence for A sending B 80 dollars.
Candidate: A confirms on a native screen, and the app saves the intent with a client transfer ID before sending.
Candidate: The server checks and moves the money in one transaction, so A goes from 100 to 20 dollars and B from 0 to 80.
Candidate: The result screen shows success only from the server's record.

[board] sequenceDiagram |     participant A as A's app |     participant S as Server ledger |     participant B as B's app |     A->>A: Save intent with client transfer ID |     A->>S: Send transfer 8000 cents, client ID |     S->>S: One transaction: debit A, credit B |     S-->>A: Transfer record: success |     A->>A: Result screen: success, A 20, B 80
Candidate: The server checks the balance and moves the money in one transaction, so A goes from 100 to 20 dollars and B from 0 to 80.
Candidate: The result screen shows success only from the server's record.
Candidate: It has four states: success, clear failure, processing, and outcome unknown while we're still checking.

Interviewer: You said the app saves the intent with a client transfer ID before sending — what exactly gets written to local storage at that moment, and how does the app use that ID when the response comes back?
Candidate: I write one row in the local database: the client transfer ID, the recipient, the amount as 8000 cents, and the status "pending".
Candidate: I write it before the request goes out, so the intent survives a crash or process death.
Candidate: When the response comes back, I look up that row by the same ID and update its status to success or failure.
Candidate: The result screen reads only from that row, so a late or duplicate response just updates the same record.
Candidate: When the response comes back, I match it to that row by the client transfer ID.
Candidate: Then I update the status to success or clear failure, and the result screen reads only from that row.
Candidate: If the response never comes, the row stays pending, so it's an unknown outcome, not a failure.
Candidate: After a restart I ask the server for that same ID, and I resend only that ID, only if the server's contract allows it.

Interviewer: Your sequence shows "S-->>A: Transfer record: success" and then the result screen reading that row — but here the server commits and the response is lost before Android kills the process. When A reopens the app, what does the user see, and how does the app resolve that pending row? Please update your sequence diagram.
Candidate: The user sees "still checking", not success and not failure.
Candidate: The result screen reads that pending row, so it shows the amount and the recipient, with a clear note that we're confirming it.
Candidate: After a restart, the app looks up the server by account and the same client transfer ID.
Candidate: If the server has the record, the row becomes success or clear failure, and the screen updates from that row.
Candidate: If the lookup finds nothing, the state stays unknown, because the request may still be in flight.

[board] sequenceDiagram |     participant A as A's app |     participant S as Server ledger |     A->>A: Restart: row still pending |     A->>S: Query by account and client ID |     S-->>A: Transfer record: success |     A->>A: Update row, show success
Candidate: The lookup has a short timeout, so a slow network can leave the row pending longer than the user expects, and in that case I show a retry button instead of guessing the outcome.

Interviewer: You said if the lookup finds nothing the state stays unknown because the request may still be in flight — but what if the server's idempotency record for that client transfer ID has already expired by the time A reopens the app?
Candidate: If the same client transfer ID comes again with the same amount and recipient, the server returns the original transfer's current status, not an error.
Candidate: If the parameters differ, it rejects the request.
Candidate: So a resend can never move the money twice.

[board] sequenceDiagram |     participant A as A's app |     participant S as Server ledger |     A->>S: Resend same client ID, 8000 cents |     S->>S: Same ID and same parameters: return original record |     S-->>A: Original transfer record: success |     A->>A: Update row, show success
Candidate: Right, so the lookup can't always answer.
Candidate: If the server has already dropped that record, I'd keep the row pending and show "still checking".
Candidate: I'd also give the user a clear way to contact support with the client transfer ID.
Candidate: The app never guesses success or failure from a missing record.

Interviewer: Separate scenario. A still has 100 dollars. On two phones A approves two independent 80 dollar transfers to B at almost the same time. What happens to each one and what do the phones show?
Candidate: These are two separate intents, each with its own client transfer ID, so they're not duplicates of one transfer.
Candidate: Each phone saves its own row as pending before sending.
Candidate: On the server, each transfer runs in one transaction with a row lock on A's balance, or a conditional update that only debits when the balance is at least 8000 cents.
Candidate: So the first one succeeds: A goes from 100 to 20 dollars and B from 0 to 80.
Candidate: The second one finds only 2000 cents left, so it fails cleanly and no money moves.
Candidate: The second one fails cleanly, so no money moves, and its pending row becomes failed.
Candidate: Both phones read only their own row, so neither shows a wrong balance.
Interviewer: Back to the first transfer. While A's request is in flight the user switches to account C, and then A's old response arrives. What could go wrong on Android and how do you prevent it?
Candidate: The old response could land on account C's screen, because the ViewModel and the list are still alive.
Candidate: So I'd tag every request and callback with the account and a session generation.
Candidate: When a response comes back, I check its session; if it's no longer current, I drop it.
Candidate: The money A already sent stays on the server, and it comes back from A's own history when A signs in again.
Candidate: The check happens in the repository, before any write, so a dropped response never touches C's row.
Candidate: A's pending row stays pending, and A's own history shows the transfer once the server record comes back.

Interviewer: You said the result screen reads only from that pending row — so if the flow now starts from a chat message like "pay Alex for last night's dinner," with two contacts named Alex and no reliable amount, what do you change before confirmation, and what happens to that pending row when the chat stream disconnects right after the user confirms?
